meta.title: NASA and ISRO Mars Mission Catalog
meta.description: Catalog of launched NASA and ISRO missions and mission groups that explored Mars, including unsuccessful attempts and spacecraft en route to Mars.

missions.name: Mariner 4
missions.objective: First successful flyby of Mars; return close-up images of the Martian surface.
missions.description: Mariner 4 performed the first successful Mars flyby on 14–15 July 1965, returning 22 close-up images. It revealed a heavily cratered, moon-like landscape and measured a thin CO₂ atmosphere.

missions.name: Mariner 6
missions.objective: Flyby study of Mars surface and atmosphere; return higher-resolution images than Mariner 4.
missions.description: Mariner 6 flew past Mars on 31 July 1969, returning 75 images of the equatorial region and studying the atmosphere with infrared and ultraviolet spectrometers.

missions.name: Mariner 7
missions.objective: Flyby of Mars to study surface and atmosphere, particularly the south polar cap.
missions.description: Mariner 7 flew past Mars on 5 August 1969, returning 126 images including coverage of the southern hemisphere and polar cap.

missions.name: Mariner 8
missions.objective: Planned Mars orbiter to map 70% of the Martian surface.
missions.description: Mariner 8 failed when its Atlas-Centaur launch vehicle malfunctioned shortly after launch on 8 May 1971.

missions.name: Mariner 9
missions.objective: First spacecraft to orbit Mars; global mapping of surface; study of atmosphere and moons.
missions.description: Mariner 9 was the first spacecraft to orbit another planet. It mapped 85% of the Martian surface and revealed Olympus Mons, Valles Marineris, and evidence of ancient riverbeds.

missions.name: Viking 1 (Orbiter + Lander)
missions.objective: First successful Mars surface landing; biology experiments; global mapping from orbit.
missions.description: Viking 1 comprised an orbiter and lander. The lander touched down in Chryse Planitia on 20 July 1976 — the first successful Mars surface operation — and operated for over six years. The orbiter mapped the surface until August 1980.

missions.name: Viking 2 (Orbiter + Lander)
missions.objective: Second Mars surface landing; biology experiments; north polar region mapping.
missions.description: Viking 2 comprised an orbiter and lander. The lander touched down in Utopia Planitia on 3 September 1976 and operated until April 1980. The orbiter operated until July 1978.

missions.name: Mars Observer
missions.objective: Global mapping of Martian surface morphology, topography, composition, gravity, and magnetic field.
missions.description: Mars Observer was lost on 21 August 1993, three days before Mars orbit insertion, likely due to a rupture in the fuel pressurisation line.

missions.name: Mars Global Surveyor
missions.objective: Global mapping of Mars surface, topography, gravity, and magnetic field.
missions.description: Mars Global Surveyor operated for over nine years and returned comprehensive maps of Mars including the foundational MOLA topographic dataset. Contact lost 2 November 2006.

missions.name: Mars Pathfinder (Lander + Sojourner Rover)
missions.objective: Demonstrate low-cost Mars landing; deploy first Mars rover; atmospheric and soil study.
missions.description: Mars Pathfinder landed in Ares Vallis using an airbag system and deployed the Sojourner rover — NASA's first Mars rover. Contact lost 27 September 1997.

missions.name: Mars Climate Orbiter
missions.objective: Study Martian climate, atmosphere, and surface changes over a full Martian year.
missions.description: Lost on 23 September 1999 when it entered the atmosphere at too low an altitude due to a metric/imperial units navigation error.

missions.name: Mars Polar Lander (with Deep Space 2 Probes)
missions.objective: Land near Mars south pole; study volatiles and climate history in polar layered deposits.
missions.description: Lost on 3 December 1999 during descent, likely due to premature engine shutdown triggered by spurious landing sensor signals. The Deep Space 2 microprobes also failed.

missions.name: Mars Odyssey
missions.objective: Map Mars chemical and mineralogical composition; detect water and buried ice.
missions.description: Mars Odyssey is the longest-operating Mars spacecraft in history, still operational as of 2026. It discovered vast hydrogen-rich (water ice) deposits and serves as a critical communications relay.

missions.name: MER-A — Spirit Rover
missions.objective: Investigate geological evidence of past water in Gusev Crater.
missions.description: Spirit operated for over six years, far exceeding its 90-sol design life. It became stuck in soft soil in May 2009; NASA declared mission end on 25 May 2011.

missions.name: MER-B — Opportunity Rover
missions.objective: Investigate geological evidence of past water activity in Meridiani Planum.
missions.description: Opportunity operated for nearly 15 years, finding definitive evidence that liquid water once existed on Mars. Contact lost 10 June 2018 during a global dust storm.

missions.name: Phoenix Mars Lander
missions.objective: Study history of water and habitability of Martian arctic soil; confirm water ice presence.
missions.description: Phoenix directly confirmed water ice in the Martian arctic, also detecting perchlorate. The mission ended in November 2008 as the Martian winter arrived.

missions.name: Mars Science Laboratory — Curiosity Rover
missions.objective: Assess Mars' habitability potential; study climate and geology in Gale Crater.
missions.description: Curiosity confirmed ancient Mars had conditions capable of supporting microbial life and continues operating in Gale Crater as of 2026.

missions.name: MAVEN
missions.objective: Investigate Mars atmospheric loss to solar wind over geological time.
missions.description: MAVEN has revealed how Mars lost most of its atmosphere to solar wind. It continues to operate as of 2026 and serves as a communications relay.

missions.name: Mars Orbiter Mission — Mangalyaan
missions.objective: Demonstrate ISRO interplanetary mission capability; study Martian surface, atmosphere, and exosphere.
missions.description: India's first interplanetary mission, developed in 15 months. India became the first Asian country to reach Mars orbit and the first to succeed on its maiden attempt. Lost contact 2 October 2022.

missions.name: Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter
missions.objective: Detailed reconnaissance of Mars; climate study; site selection for future missions.
missions.description: MRO carries HiRISE, the most powerful camera ever sent to another planet, and has returned more data than all other Mars missions combined. Still operational as of 2026.

missions.name: InSight Mars Lander
missions.objective: Study interior structure and thermal state of Mars.
missions.description: InSight detected over 1,300 marsquakes and studied Mars' interior layers. Contact lost 15 December 2022 as dust covered its solar panels.

missions.name: Mars 2020 — Perseverance Rover + Ingenuity Helicopter
missions.objective: Seek signs of ancient life; collect samples for Mars Sample Return; test oxygen production; first powered flight on Mars.
missions.description: Perseverance landed in Jezero Crater carrying the Ingenuity helicopter. Ingenuity completed 72 flights before rotor damage in January 2024. Perseverance continues collecting samples as of 2026.

missions.name: Mariner 3
missions.objective: Attempt a Mars flyby and conduct interplanetary science observations.
missions.description: The payload shroud failed to separate, and the spacecraft lost power before it could enter a proper Mars-transfer trajectory. It never reached Mars.

missions.name: Mars Cube One (MarCO-A and MarCO-B)
missions.objective: Demonstrate interplanetary CubeSats and relay InSight entry, descent, and landing data to Earth.
missions.description: The twin CubeSats flew past Mars during InSight’s landing and relayed its telemetry in near real time. MarCO-B also returned an image of Mars during the flyby.

missions.name: ESCAPADE (Twin Mars Orbiters)
missions.objective: Study how the solar wind interacts with Mars’ magnetosphere and contributes to atmospheric escape.
missions.description: NASA’s twin spacecraft launched on 13 November 2025 and are en route to Mars. NASA currently plans Mars orbit insertion in September 2027.
